title: Variations in Temperature, pH, and Osmotic Pressure contribute to changes in Pseudomonas aeruginosa autofluorescence via mechanisms involving regulation of the pvdD/pvdS gene
content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a bacteria that is frequently detected in chronic wounds. Bacterial infection can impede wound healing and, in severe cases, result in fatalities. Bacterial fluorescence imaging is a technique used to detect the cyan fluorescence emitted by P. aeruginosa, thereby assisting clinicians in improving wound treatment. Our previous observations revealed an intriguing phenomenon whereby bacteria exhibited distinct fluorescence characteristics despite the presence of an identical bacterial load in the wound. To investigate whether these alterations in fluorescence intensity were influenced by varying bacterial environments, we conducted a study using image J software to analyze the changes in fluorescence intensity of P. aeruginosa colonies under different conditions, including temperatures (25°C, 31°C, 37°C, 43°C), pH levels (5, 6, 7, 8, 9), and osmotic pressures (0.9%, 1.8%, 2.7%, 3.6%). Additionally, we assessed the expression levels of pyoverdine synthetase genes (pvdD) and the sigma factor of pyoverdine genes (pvdS), which determine the fluorescence intensity of P. aeruginosa under these varying conditions. Our experimental findings demonstrated that the bacterial fluorescence intensity was significantly influenced by the culture environment, with the ability to be enhanced or attenuated by modifying the growth conditions. Moreover, there was a strong correlation between the fluorescence intensity of the bacteria and the expression level of key enzyme genes. Consequently, when implementing fluorescence imaging systems in clinical settings, it is essential to consider the changes in the wound microenvironment.
